issues.legal_issue: A bill is duly passed when the Speaker certifies that it was passed, despite the official proceedings omitting a record that the final motion was put and carried.
material_facts: The Assembly considered the bill through its final reading, and the proceedings recorded the motion that it be passed and speeches supporting it without recording a final vote or declaration that it carried.
The Speaker certified on the printed bill that it had been passed; that certification was made before the Speaker later signed the printed proceedings.
The speeches and the course of the Assembly proceedings disclosed no opposition to passing the bill.
issues.conclusion: The Speaker’s certificate was conclusive proof that the bill was passed, and the omission in the proceedings did not invalidate the Act; in any event, any failure formally to put the motion was only a procedural irregularity.
issues.legal_principle: The Speaker’s authentication of a bill as passed is conclusive evidence of passage, consistently with the parliamentary practice described in Craies’ Statute Law and May’s Parliamentary Practice. The Court also treated any procedural omission as an irregularity rather than a defect invalidating the enactment, referring to article 212 of the Constitution.

rule.if: challenge_to_enacted_law and speaker_certified_passage and (proceedings_omit_final_vote_record or final_vote_not_formally_put) and no_opposition_to_bill

predicates.challenge_to_enacted_law: A party challenges the validity of an enacted law on the ground that the legislature did not pass the bill.
predicates.speaker_certified_passage: The Speaker certified that the bill was passed by the legislature.
predicates.proceedings_omit_final_vote_record: The official proceedings do not record that the final motion was put to a vote or carried.
predicates.final_vote_not_formally_put: The final motion may not have been formally put to the legislature.
predicates.no_opposition_to_bill: The proceedings and speeches showed no opposition to the bill being passed.

issues.definition: When an enacted law is challenged over its passage, the Speaker certified passage and the record omits or may omit a final vote, the absence of opposition supports treating passage as valid.

issues.legal_issue: A state bill reserved for the President’s consideration may become law upon presidential assent without prior gubernatorial assent or a second reservation for presidential consideration.
material_facts: After the Assembly passed the bill, the Governor reserved it for the President’s consideration rather than first assenting to it.
The President assented to the bill, which was then published as an Act.
issues.conclusion: The President’s assent was sufficient; the Constitution did not require prior assent by the Governor or a second reservation and assent.
issues.legal_principle: Articles 31(3) and 31(4), read with articles 200 and 201 of the Constitution, allow the Governor to reserve a passed bill for the President and the President to assent to it. The President may perform the relevant functions at the same time, and the term “Legislature” in article 31(4) refers to the legislative House or Houses, not the Governor.

rule.if: challenge_to_enacted_law and bill_passed_by_state_house and governor_reserved_bill and president_assented and no_prior_governor_assent

predicates.challenge_to_enacted_law: A party challenges the validity or effect of an enacted law.
predicates.bill_passed_by_state_house: The state legislative House passed the bill.
predicates.governor_reserved_bill: The Governor reserved the passed bill for the President’s consideration.
predicates.president_assented: The President assented to the bill.
predicates.no_prior_governor_assent: The Governor did not first assent to the bill before reserving it.

issues.definition: When a state House has passed a bill that the Governor reserves and the President assents to, the absence of prior gubernatorial assent does not prevent enactment.

issues.legal_issue: The adequacy of compensation under a qualifying acquisition law cannot be judicially examined when the constitutional protections governing such laws apply.
material_facts: The challenged law provided compensation calculated under statutory schedules and payable in cash or bonds, potentially in instalments.
The petitioners alleged that the compensation was substantially below the value and income of their property and was therefore inadequate or illusory.
The bill was pending at the commencement of the Constitution, was reserved for the President’s consideration, and received his assent; the Act was also included in the Ninth Schedule.
issues.conclusion: The Court had no jurisdiction to inquire into the adequacy of compensation, and the compensation provisions were not illusory on the facts described.
issues.legal_principle: Articles 31(4), 31-A and 31-B barred an inquiry into the challenge to compensation based on inconsistency with fundamental rights. Article 31(4) applied because the bill was pending at the commencement of the Constitution, was reserved, and received presidential assent; the First Amendment protections also applied to the Act. The Court distinguished inadequate compensation from compensation that was merely illusory, noting that the statute provided for a positive amount.

rule.if: constitutional_challenge_proceeding and compulsory_property_acquisition and qualifying_constitutional_protection_applies and compensation_is_provided

predicates.constitutional_challenge_proceeding: A party brings a constitutional challenge to a law authorizing acquisition of property.
predicates.compulsory_property_acquisition: The challenged law transfers private property to the State by compulsory acquisition.
predicates.qualifying_constitutional_protection_app: The law satisfies the constitutional conditions that protect it from challenge based on fundamental rights.
predicates.compensation_is_provided: The law provides a positive amount of compensation rather than no compensation at all.

issues.definition: When a constitutional challenge concerns compulsory acquisition, a qualifying constitutional protection applies, and the law provides compensation, the adequacy of that compensation is not judicially reviewed.

issues.legal_issue: The acquisition of proprietary interests under the challenged land-reform law served a public purpose and was within the legislature’s authority, and the compensation scheme did not establish a fraud on the Constitution or an impermissible delegation of essential legislative power.
material_facts: The law acquired intermediary proprietary interests to bring cultivators into direct contact with the State, transfer specified interests and management functions, and reform the land-tenure system.
The law set out statutory methods for calculating compensation and provided for rules concerning payment by instalments and interim payments.

The petitioners argued that the reform lacked a public purpose, that the compensation was illusory, that the enactment was designed to evade constitutional guarantees, and that it delegated essential legislative functions.
The Court found that compensation was payable in every case and that the law’s reform purposes benefited the public.
issues.conclusion: The Court rejected the challenges based on absence of public purpose, lack of legislative competence, fraud on the Constitution, and delegation of essential legislative power.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the legislative subject of acquisition and requisition of property in entry 36 of List II and the acquisition and requisition subject in entry 42 of List III, together with articles 31(2), 31(4), 31-A and 31-B. It relied on its reasoning in the Bihar appeals concerning these objections, finding a public purpose in land-tenure reform and no improper delegation or fraudulent design. It also held that the constitutional bar on reviewing compensation foreclosed a challenge based on inadequacy.

rule.if: constitutional_challenge_proceeding and land_reform_acquisition and acquisition_connects_cultivators_with_state and compensation_formula_provides_positive_payment and statutory_scheme_sets_compensation_method

predicates.constitutional_challenge_proceeding: A party challenges the constitutionality of a law authorizing compulsory acquisition.
predicates.land_reform_acquisition: The law acquires proprietary interests as part of a reform of land tenure.
predicates.acquisition_connects_cultivators_with_st: The law aims to bring cultivators into direct contact with the State by eliminating intermediaries.
predicates.compensation_formula_provides_positive_p: The compensation formula yields a positive payment rather than zero or a negative amount.
predicates.statutory_scheme_sets_compensation_metho: The law itself establishes the method for calculating compensation and provides for implementation through rules.

issues.definition: When an acquisition law reforms land tenure by connecting cultivators directly with the State and supplies a statutory compensation method yielding a positive payment, those features do not establish invalidity on the stated grounds.

issues.legal_issue: A law specifically protected by the constitutional schedule may remain valid as applied to land that does not fall within the constitutional definition of an estate.
material_facts: The law was specified in the Ninth Schedule.
Some acquired malguzari villages were accepted as falling outside the relevant statutory definition of an estate.
The petitioners argued that the constitutional protection for estates therefore did not protect acquisition of those villages.
issues.conclusion: Article 31-B independently validated the Act in respect of the malguzari villages, and article 31(4) also saved the law in its entirety.
issues.legal_principle: Article 31-B is an independent provision and is not merely illustrative of or limited by article 31-A, notwithstanding its opening words, “without prejudice to the generality” of article 31-A. The Court relied on King Emperor v. Sibnath Banerjee for the distinction between an independent provision and one that merely illustrates another provision, and held that article 31(4) was not confined to estates.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_proceeding: A party challenges the application of a law on constitutional grounds.
predicates.law_listed_for_constitutional_protection: The challenged law is specifically included among laws receiving constitutional protection.
predicates.acquired_land_outside_estate_definition: The acquired land does not fall within the relevant constitutional definition of an estate.

issues.definition: When a challenged law is specifically constitutionally protected, that protection extends to acquired land even if the land is outside the relevant definition of an estate.

issues.legal_issue: A covenant recognizing a ruler’s property as private property does not prevent the State from acquiring that property under a law of general application.
material_facts: The covenant of merger recognized certain properties as the ruler’s private properties rather than State properties.
The challenged law treated the properties as private property and sought to acquire them along with other proprietary interests.
The petitioners relied on the constitutional assurance concerning rulers’ personal rights, privileges and dignities.
issues.conclusion: Article 362 did not prohibit acquisition of the recognized private properties or guarantee their perpetual existence.
issues.legal_principle: Article 362 requires due regard to relevant guarantees or assurances concerning a ruler’s personal rights, privileges and dignities; it does not prevent acquisition of property recognized as private or guarantee that property against acquisition. The Court also referred to article 363 as barring judicial determination of disputes arising out of the covenant.

predicates.challenge_based_on_merger_covenant: A party challenges acquisition by relying on a covenant made in connection with a merger.
predicates.covenant_recognizes_private_property: The covenant recognizes the property as the ruler’s private property rather than State property.
predicates.state_law_acquires_property_as_private: The State law acquires the property on the basis that it is private property.

issues.definition: When a merger covenant recognizes property as private and a State law acquires it on that basis, the recognition does not itself bar acquisition.

issues.legal_issue: Courts lack jurisdiction to decide disputes arising out of a covenant or agreement of merger.
material_facts: The petitioners’ challenge to acquisition of property depended on the terms and effect of a covenant of merger.
The Court considered the constitutional bar on judicial determination of disputes arising out of such covenants.
issues.conclusion: The jurisdiction of the Court to decide disputes arising out of the covenant of merger was barred.
issues.legal_principle: Article 363 of the Constitution bars the jurisdiction of courts over disputes arising out of specified treaties, agreements, covenants, engagements and similar instruments. The judgment states that the bar independently foreclosed judicial determination of the covenant dispute.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_proceeding: A party brings a constitutional challenge involving property recognized under a merger arrangement.
predicates.claim_depends_on_merger_covenant: The party’s claim depends on the terms or effect of a covenant of merger.
predicates.dispute_arises_from_covenant: The dispute arises out of the covenant or agreement itself.

issues.definition: When a claim in a constitutional challenge depends on a merger covenant and the dispute arises from that covenant, the court lacks jurisdiction to decide the covenant dispute.
